A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v2's added experimental material.

before.justification: v1 presents theoretical results and proofs, including in its appendices. Figure 1 is an illustrative schematic; the experiments discussed elsewhere belong to cited work.

after.justification: Figures 2–3 report original synthetic classification experiments with finite-step gradient descent. Appendix E describes their implementation and evaluation over 2,500 tasks.

M1.justification: The convex single-layer linear transformer, prediction rule (3.2), and gradient-descent objectives remain unchanged. The added experiments instantiate the existing method without introducing a new component.

E1.justification: v1 has no empirical dataset coverage. v2 introduces actual training and evaluation on synthetic Gaussian-mixture binary classification tasks with clean pretraining and noisy in-context labels, empirically studying the previously theoretical task family.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates a competing method. Figures 2–3 add a theoretical 'Optimal Test (0.80)' reference alongside the transformer's training and test accuracies, without an evaluated baseline algorithm.

E3.justification: v2 introduces an experimental protocol absent from v1: 300 full-batch gradient-descent steps, learning rate 0.01, N=40 pretraining examples per task, and evaluation with context length 20 and label-flipping rate 0.2. Figures 2–3 vary dimension, pretraining task count, and signal strength.

E4.justification: Figures 2–3 introduce sensitivity studies over dimension and pretraining task count, using test signal scalings d^0.1, d^0.3, and d^0.6. They examine when memorization coexists with generalization and how task requirements depend on signal strength; v1 contains no corresponding empirical analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix E adds task-level averaging over 2,500 evaluation tasks and one-standard-error bars, absent from v1. This introduces a standard uncertainty summary; independent pretraining repetitions and random seeds are not specified.

E6.justification: v2 adds the first empirical results. Figure 2 shows memorization with poor generalization at weak signal, training accuracy approaching 1 with test accuracy near 0.80 at intermediate signal, and both near 0.80 at strong signal. Figure 3 adds task-count-dependent accuracy trends.

T1.justification: The main assumptions and theorem statements remain unchanged. However, v2's Appendix C.6 newly calls R(WMM) clean-example error, creating an inconsistency with the retained noisy-label definition (4.1). Lemma C.5 also newly mixes W with the quantified matrix Q. These are local formal inconsistencies, not new theoretical results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: task/sample complexity guarantees and benign in-context overfitting for the restricted linear transformer. The experiments supply evidence for these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new experiments as evidence that finite-step training exhibits the asymptotic theory's behavior. Its conclusion also explains why noisy pretraining could make the max-margin constraints infeasible, and why generalization remains unclear even when noisy labels can be memorized.

D1.justification: New Appendix E provides the first experimental implementation and reproduction information: PyTorch, zero initialization, training parameters, accuracy computation, NVIDIA RTX 3500 Ada hardware, runtime guidance, and a code-repository link. v1 provides no corresponding experimental recipe or code-access statement.

R1.justification: The cited works, related-work discussion, and principal novelty positioning are retained. The expanded setting paragraph reiterates the existing contrast between prior linear-regression work and this paper's classification setting.

P1.justification: v2 adds localized explanatory prose about the task distribution, experiments, and noisy-pretraining limitations, plus Appendix E and acknowledgements. The overall narrative, section sequence, and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds two three-panel experimental figures with accuracy curves, error bars, and optimal-test reference lines, plus Table 1 summarizing notation. These substantially expand the visual presentation; the original schematic remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: Figures 2–3 usefully connect the asymptotic theory to finite-step training, supported by uncertainty reporting and reproducibility details. The notation table and expanded limitation discussion also help readers. These improve an otherwise largely unchanged theoretical contribution, although the new risk-definition and Q/W inconsistencies in Appendix C temper the gains.
